output.answer: Helpfulness and harmlessness pull against each other in RLHF-trained assistants. A preference model trained mainly on one quality scores much worse than chance on the other, and an excessive focus on either quality produces either evasive or harmful replies. The authors reduce the tension by training preference models on a mixture of both datasets, which they report works, and they find that larger preference models become more robust to the mix. They also use OOD detection to reject strange and harmful requests.

claims.text: There is a tension between helpfulness and harmlessness in RLHF-trained assistants, measurable in both preference models and RLHF policies.
claims.quote: There is a tension between helpfulness and harmlessness, which can be measured at the level of both preference modeling and RLHF-trained policies (Figure 1).

claims.text: Preference models trained on one quality perform very poorly on the other.
claims.quote: We demonstrate this tension quantitatively by showing that preference models trained to primarily evaluate one of these qualities perform very poorly (much worse than chance) on the other.

claims.text: Overemphasizing harm avoidance produces unhelpful safe responses.
claims.quote: An excessive focus on avoiding harm can lead to ‘safe’ responses that don’t actually address the needs of the human.

claims.text: Training preference models on a mixture of helpful and harmless data reduces the tension.
claims.quote: Fortunately, we find that PMs trained on a mixture of both datasets can nevertheless learn the right lessons and behave helpfully when appropriate, while encouraging the polite refusal of harmful requests.

claims.text: Larger preference models become much more robust to the mix of helpful and harmless training data.
claims.quote: as model size increases, PMs perform better on both distributions simultaneously and become much more robust to the relative proportions of helpful and harmless training data.

claims.text: OOD detection can reject most strange and harmful requests.
claims.quote: We also show that one can use OOD detection techniques [Fort et al., 2021] to reject most strange and harmful requests (Figure 22), with little or no harmful examples (Figure 23).

output.answer: Language models do not use long contexts evenly. Performance is often lowest when the relevant information sits in the middle of the input, and moving it degrades results significantly. Extra retrieved passages add cost and can lower accuracy: in the open-domain QA case study, reader accuracy saturates after about 20 documents while retriever recall keeps rising. The library does not give a direct accuracy-versus-distractor curve, so the distractor point rests on the trade-off the authors describe.

claims.text: Performance degrades when relevant information moves away from the start or end of a long context, and it is often lowest in the middle.
claims.quote: In particular, performance is often lowest when models must use information in the middle of long input contexts.

claims.text: Changing the position of relevant information degrades language model performance significantly.
claims.quote: We show that language model performance degrades significantly when changing the position of relevant information, indicating that models struggle to robustly access and use information in long input contexts.

claims.text: Adding more context can help, but it also raises the amount of content the model must reason over.
claims.quote: providing the language model with more information may help it perform the downstream task, but it also increases the amount of content that the model must reason over, potentially decreasing accuracy.

claims.text: Beyond about 20 retrieved documents, extra passages add little accuracy and substantial cost.
claims.quote: Using more than 20 retrieved documents only marginally improves reader performance (∼1.5% for GPT-3.5Turbo and ∼1% for Claude-1.3), while significantly increasing the input context length (and thus latency and cost).

claims.text: Reader accuracy saturates long before retriever recall, so readers do not use the extra retrieved context well.
claims.quote: We see that reader model performance saturates long before retriever performance saturates, indicating that readers are not effectively using the extra context.

output.answer: The Jailbroken paper names two failure modes of safety training: competing objectives, where instruction following or pretraining pulls against refusal, and mismatched generalization, where safety training does not cover capabilities the base model has. Automated attacks exploit this indirectly. The adaptive-attack paper runs random search over an adversarial suffix to maximize the logprob of a target token such as “Sure”, and it reports 100% success on several open models. The library does not tie the automated method to the two failure modes by name, so that link is my inference.

claims.text: Safety-trained models are trained against several objectives that can conflict.
claims.quote: Competing objectives stems from the observation that safety-trained LLMs are typically trained against multiple objectives that can conflict with each other.

claims.text: Prompts can force a choice between restricted behavior and a penalized response.
claims.quote: This training can be exploited by crafting prompts that force a choice between either a restricted behavior or a response that is heavily penalized by the pretraining and instruction following objectives.

claims.text: Pretraining covers more capabilities than safety training does, which creates mismatched generalization.
claims.quote: Our second failure mode comes from observing that pretraining is done on a larger and more diverse dataset than safety training, and thus the model has many capabilities not covered by safety training.

claims.text: Vulnerabilities persist despite extensive red-teaming and safety-training efforts.
claims.quote: We find that vulnerabilities persist despite the extensive red-teaming and safety-training efforts behind these models.

claims.text: The automated attack optimizes an adversarial suffix with random search on a target logprob.
claims.quote: we initially design an adversarial prompt template (sometimes adapted to the target LLM), and then we apply random search on a suffix to maximize a target logprob (e.g., of the token “Sure”), potentially with multiple restarts.

claims.text: The automated attack reaches 100% success on several models, judged by GPT-4.
claims.quote: In this way, we achieve 100% attack success rate—according to GPT-4 as a judge—on Vicuna-13B, Mistral-7B, Phi-3-Mini, Nemotron-4-340B, Llama-2-Chat-7B/13B/70B, Llama-3-Instruct-8B, Gemma-7B, GPT-3.5, GPT-4o, and R2D2 from HarmBench that was adversarially trained against the GCG attack.

output.answer: Attackers plant instructions in content that the application retrieves, such as web pages or documents, and the model treats them as instructions. The paper calls this Indirect Prompt Injection. The authors show it against Bing's GPT-4 powered Chat and code-completion engines, where injected prompts can manipulate the application and control other API calls.

claims.text: LLM-integrated applications blur the line between data and instructions.
claims.quote: We argue that LLM-Integrated Applications blur the line between data and instructions.

claims.text: Indirect prompt injection lets adversaries exploit applications remotely by injecting prompts into data that is likely to be retrieved.
claims.quote: We reveal new attack vectors, using Indirect Prompt Injection, that enable adversaries to remotely (without a direct interface) exploit LLM-integrated applications by strategically injecting prompts into data likely to be retrieved.

claims.text: The attacks work against real-world systems such as Bing's GPT-4 powered Chat and code-completion engines.
claims.quote: We demonstrate our attacks’ practical viability against both real-world systems, such as Bing’s GPT-4 powered Chat and code-completion engines, and synthetic applications built on GPT-4.

claims.text: Processing retrieved prompts can manipulate the application and control other API calls.
claims.quote: We show how processing retrieved prompts can act as arbitrary code execution, manipulate the application’s functionality, and control how and if other APIs are called.

output.answer: Reflexion lets language agents improve across trials without changing their weights. After each attempt, the agent reflects on the feedback in words and keeps those reflections in an episodic memory buffer that shapes later trials. The abstract reports 91% pass@1 on HumanEval, above the 80% of the GPT-4 baseline it cites.

claims.text: Reflexion improves agents through linguistic feedback rather than weight updates.
claims.quote: We propose Reflexion, a novel framework to reinforce language agents not by updating weights, but instead through linguistic feedback.

claims.text: Reflexion agents keep verbal reflections in an episodic memory buffer that guides later trials.
claims.quote: Concretely, Reflexion agents verbally reflect on task feedback signals, then maintain their own reflective text in an episodic memory buffer to induce better decision-making in subsequent trials.

claims.text: Reflexion reaches 91% pass@1 on HumanEval, above the GPT-4 baseline of 80%.
claims.quote: For example, Reflexion achieves a 91% pass@1 accuracy on the HumanEval coding benchmark, surpassing the previous state-of-the-art GPT-4 that achieves 80%.

output.answer: Parameters store popular facts well but struggle with long-tail facts, and scaling mainly helps popular knowledge. Retrieval augmentation helps significantly on less popular entities. The authors use this to propose retrieving non-parametric memories only when needed, which improves performance and lowers inference cost.

claims.text: Language models struggle with less popular factual knowledge, and retrieval augmentation helps in those cases.
claims.quote: We find that LMs struggle with less popular factual knowledge, and that retrieval augmentation helps significantly in these cases.

claims.text: Scaling mainly improves memorization of popular knowledge and does little for the long tail.
claims.quote: Scaling, on the other hand, mainly improves memorization of popular knowledge, and fails to appreciably improve memorization of factual knowledge in the long tail.

claims.text: Retrieving non-parametric memories only when necessary improves performance and reduces inference cost.
claims.quote: Based on those findings, we devise a new method for retrieval augmentation that improves performance and reduces inference costs by only retrieving non-parametric memories when necessary.
